cur:catacombs-arles-jonah.summary: Two registers of figures surround a shell with the portraits of a couple; the lower register is filled by the sea and the story of Jonah, while elsewhere Christ appears among the apostles performing miracles. Jonah's deliverance, a sign of the resurrection, is joined to the miracles of Christ.
facts: The museum names it after the story of Jonah, which occupies much of the lower register.
Its two-register layout with a central shell is the Roman type also seen on the Dogmatic Sarcophagus.
cur:catacombs-arles-jonah.notes: Date approximate; the Christ scenes were not individually verified.

cur:catacombs-leiden-rubens-sarcophagus.summary: Five arched niches on twisted columns each frame a New Testament scene with Christ – among them his miracles of healing and his encounters with his disciples. The calm, classical figures are typical of late-4th-century Rome.
facts: Commons records that this sarcophagus once belonged to the painter Peter Paul Rubens.
It is now in the Rijksmuseum van Oudheden (National Museum of Antiquities) in Leiden.
cur:catacombs-leiden-rubens-sarcophagus.notes: The five scenes were not identified individually here.

cur:manuscripts-paris-gregory-christ-amo.summary: At the top the boy Christ sits enthroned behind a table in the Temple between seated teachers, while Joseph and Mary arrive at the left; at the right the adult Christ stands apart. The middle register shows Christ performing healings beside a tall building, and at the bottom he stands between two apostles blessing the loaves as baskets of bread are filled and the crowd sits on the grass.
facts: The Paris Gregory was commissioned by Patriarch Photios as a gift for Emperor Basil I between 879 and 883 and is one of the most ambitious Byzantine manuscripts to survive from the generation after Iconoclasm.
Many of its full-page miniatures do not illustrate Gregory's sermons directly but set biblical and historical scenes beside them as a commentary devised for the court.
cur:manuscripts-paris-gregory-christ-amo.notes: Folio derived from the Gallica image sequence (view number minus 13, halved) and checked against folios named on other Commons files of this manuscript. The upper and middle registers are badly flaked; the middle scene is not identified.

cur:manuscripts-drogo-christ-with-apostl.summary: Framed by the bowl of a gold-and-green letter D, Christ stands haloed at the centre of a small grassy rise, turning and gesturing toward a group of apostles on either side who lean in to listen. The sketch-like figures, painted in soft greens, browns and violets, give a vivid sense of conversation.
facts: The Drogo Sacramentary was written and painted for the personal use of Drogo, Bishop of Metz and a son of Charlemagne; it contains only the prayers spoken by the bishop at Mass through the year.
Its scenes are set inside the initial letters of the prayers, in delicate gold vine-scrolls — an early and influential use of the historiated initial.
cur:manuscripts-drogo-christ-with-apostl.notes: Folio not stated on the Commons file; the miniature is an initial within the text page. The exact episode is not identified on the source; the subject is described as 'Christ teaching'.

cur:manuscripts-athelstan-psalter-christ.summary: Within a double mandorla Christ sits enthroned, raising his right hand between the letters Alpha and Omega and holding a tall cross. Around him, in an outer mandorla, rows of faces are labelled as the choirs of martyrs, confessors and virgins. The page depicts the saints of every rank gathered before the risen Christ.
facts: The Athelstan Psalter is a 9th-century Carolingian psalter to which full-page miniatures were added in England in the 10th century; it is traditionally associated with King Æthelstan, and one of its leaves is now in the Bodleian Library, Oxford (MS Rawl. B 484).
The labels 'omnis chorus martyrum', 'confessorum' and 'virginum' run around the outer mandorla.

cur:objects3-romsey-st-annes-rood.summary: This small limestone panel shows Christ crucified with a halo, between two angels above the cross-arm and two haloed mourners, usually taken to be the Virgin Mary and St John. Below them two figures raise the spear and the sponge on long shafts, and leafy scrolls spring up beside the foot of the cross. It is a distinct work from the larger 'Romsey Rood' on the outside wall of the abbey, and one of the most complete Anglo-Saxon Crucifixion carvings to survive in England.
facts: Romsey Abbey describes it as a low-relief carving of the Crucifixion on a block of limestone, probably of the 10th century, now framed by an altar consecrated in 2015.
King Edgar refounded (or founded) the nunnery at Romsey in 967 under the Rule of St Benedict, the period to which local tradition links the carving.
cur:objects3-romsey-st-annes-rood.notes: Not the same work as the large external Romsey Rood already in the collection (wga:m/master/yunk_en/00cross). The figure identifications are inferred from the iconography; the date is given by the abbey as 'probably 10th century'.
